title: Interpreting the Bible
summary: A practical guide to reading any Bible passage accurately: observe, interpret, apply.
description: Hermeneutics is the art and science of interpretation. This course teaches a simple, reliable method for understanding Scripture: observing what the text says, interpreting it in its context and kind of writing, letting Scripture explain Scripture, and applying it faithfully. It also shows how to handle the Old Testament, parables, prophecy and letters, and how to avoid common mistakes.
objectives: Teach a clear three-step method: observation, interpretation, application
Show how context, grammar and history shape meaning
Explain how to read different kinds of biblical writing
Warn against common errors in interpretation
outcomes: Ask good observation questions of any passage
Explain a verse in its literary and historical context
Read narrative, poetry, prophecy, parables and letters appropriately
Recognise and avoid proof-texting and allegorising
Apply a passage faithfully to life today

modules.title: Why Interpretation Matters
modules.intro: Everyone interprets the Bible. This week we see why careful interpretation is a duty for every believer.

lessons.title: Rightly dividing the word
lessons.body:
Paul tells Timothy to be "a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Timothy 2:15). The picture is of a craftsman cutting straight. Handling the Bible well takes care and skill.

Peter warns that some "wrest" (twist) Paul's letters "unto their own destruction" (2 Peter 3:16). False teachers usually quote the Bible; they simply misread it.

The goal of interpretation is to discover what God meant by what He said through the human author, not what we would like it to mean.

lessons.title: The Spirit and the student
lessons.body:
We need both the Holy Spirit and careful study. "The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:14). The Spirit illuminates the humble believer.

Yet the Spirit does not replace reading. The Bereans searched the Scriptures (Acts 17:11); Ezra "prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:10).

Pray before you read, read carefully, and be willing to obey what you find. A heart unwilling to obey will struggle to understand (John 7:17).

lessons.title: One meaning, many applications
lessons.body:
A sound rule is that each passage has one main intended meaning, given by God through its author, but may have many applications.

For example, Philippians 4:13, "I can do all things through Christ", means in context that Paul can be content in plenty or hunger by Christ's strength (Philippians 4:11-12). It applies to many situations of contentment and endurance; it is not a promise that we can achieve any ambition we choose.

Meaning is fixed by the text; applications must grow out of that meaning.

terms.def: The principles and methods of interpreting Scripture.
Drawing the meaning out of a text by careful study.
Reading one's own ideas into a text; the opposite of exegesis.
What God meant to communicate through the human writer.
A text's one fixed sense, and the many ways it can rightly be lived out.
To twist the Scriptures away from their true sense.

texts.teaches: God's workman must handle the word of truth accurately.
Some twist the Scriptures to their own destruction.
Prepare the heart to seek, do and teach God's law.
A willingness to do God's will helps us know the truth of the teaching.
Christ gives strength to be content in every circumstance.

summary: Interpretation is a duty: we must handle God's Word accurately.
We need the Spirit's illumination and diligent study together.
Seek the author's intended meaning, not our own ideas.
One meaning, many faithful applications.

questions.q: What is eisegesis?
options: Reading one's own ideas into the text
Drawing meaning out of the text

questions.q: In context, Philippians 4:13 is mainly about:
options: Contentment and endurance through Christ's strength

questions.q: Which is true about the Holy Spirit and Bible study?
options: The Spirit illuminates, but we must still study carefully

questions.q: According to 2 Peter 3:16, what do the unstable do with Scripture?

modules.title: Observation: What Does It Say?
modules.intro: Good interpretation starts by looking carefully. This week we practise observation.

lessons.title: Read slowly, ask questions
lessons.body:
Observation means noticing what is actually in the text before deciding what it means. Read the passage several times, ideally in one sitting with its chapter.

Ask the reporter's questions: **Who** is speaking and to whom? **What** is happening? **When** and **where**? **Why** is it said? **How** does it unfold?

Psalm 119:18 is a good prayer: "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law." Many errors come not from deep theology but from not reading what is there.

lessons.title: Key words and connections
lessons.body:
Look for **repeated words**: "love" in 1 Corinthians 13, "better" in Hebrews, "believe" in John.

Watch **connecting words**: *therefore* (a conclusion), *but* (a contrast), *for* or *because* (a reason), *that* or *so that* (a purpose). Romans 12:1 begins "I beseech you therefore", pointing back to the mercies of God in chapters 1 to 11.

Note **commands, promises, warnings and lists**, and any comparisons such as "like" or "as". These are the joints of the passage.

lessons.title: Seeing the structure
lessons.body:
Most passages have a flow. A letter may move from greeting to prayer to teaching to application. A story has setting, conflict, climax and outcome. A psalm may move from complaint to trust.

Try to outline the passage in a few lines. Ephesians, for example, moves from what God has done (chapters 1 to 3) to how believers should walk (chapters 4 to 6, beginning "walk worthy" in 4:1).

Seeing the structure keeps us from lifting one sentence out of its place.

terms.def: Carefully noticing what a text actually says before interpreting it.
Words used several times that often reveal a passage's theme.
Words such as therefore, but and because that show logical links.
The outline or flow of a passage.
Who, what, when, where, why and how.
A command in the text.

texts.teaches: Ask God to open our eyes to see wonders in His law.
Jesus asked, 'What is written? how readest thou?'
'Therefore' links Christian living to God's mercies.
John states his purpose: that you might believe and have life.
Believers are urged to walk worthy of their calling.

summary: Observe before you interpret: read slowly and repeatedly.
Ask who, what, when, where, why and how.
Notice repeated words and connecting words such as therefore and but.
Outline the passage to see its flow.

questions.q: What does the word "therefore" usually signal?
options: A conclusion drawn from what came before

questions.q: Which question belongs to observation?
options: Who is speaking and to whom?
How should I apply this at work?
What would I prefer it to mean?

questions.q: Ephesians 1-3 and 4-6 can be summarised as:
options: What God has done; how believers should walk

questions.q: John 20:31 is helpful because it states:

modules.title: Interpretation: What Does It Mean?
modules.intro: This week we learn the main rules for finding the meaning: context, history, grammar and Scripture interpreting Scripture.

lessons.title: Context is king
lessons.body:
A verse must be read in its **context**: the sentence, the paragraph, the chapter, the book, and the whole Bible.

Take Revelation 3:20: "I stand at the door, and knock." In context, Christ is speaking to a lukewarm church at Laodicea, calling it back to fellowship (Revelation 3:14-22). It is often used in evangelism, and the principle of Christ's invitation is true, but its first meaning is a call to a church.

A text without a context easily becomes a pretext for whatever we want it to say.

lessons.title: History, culture and grammar
lessons.body:
The Bible was written in real times and places. Knowing that Samaritans and Jews despised each other makes the Good Samaritan shocking (Luke 10:30-37; John 4:9). Knowing that Philippi was a Roman colony helps us read "our conversation (citizenship) is in heaven" (Philippians 3:20).

Grammar matters too: who does what to whom, and when. In Ephesians 2:8, "by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves", salvation as a whole is God's gift.

A good study Bible, Bible dictionary and atlas are useful tools.

lessons.title: Scripture interprets Scripture
lessons.body:
Because the whole Bible has one divine Author, it does not contradict itself. Clearer passages help us understand harder ones.

For example, James 2:24 says a man is justified by works. Romans 3:28 says by faith without works. Reading both in context shows that Paul speaks of how we are declared righteous before God (by faith alone), while James speaks of how true faith is shown before others (by works). Both agree: saving faith is a working faith.

Always gather all that Scripture says before forming a doctrine.

terms.def: The surrounding text and setting that determine a passage's meaning.
The time, place, customs and events behind a passage.
Interpreting a text by its plain grammar and historical setting.
Interpreting Scripture in harmony with the rest of Scripture.
A false reason; what a text becomes when torn from its context.
Another passage on the same subject that helps explain a text.

texts.teaches: Christ calls a lukewarm church back to fellowship with Him.
Jews had no dealings with the Samaritans.
A man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
True faith is shown to be real by works.
Believers are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.

summary: Read every verse in its context: sentence, book and whole Bible.
History, culture and grammar shape meaning.
Scripture interprets Scripture; clear passages explain hard ones.
Gather all the Bible says before forming a doctrine.

questions.q: To whom is Revelation 3:20 first addressed?
options: The disciples at the Last Supper

questions.q: How do Paul (Romans 3:28) and James (James 2:24) agree?
options: Saving faith is a working faith

questions.q: Why is the Good Samaritan story shocking in its setting?
options: Jews and Samaritans despised each other

questions.q: The analogy of faith means:
options: Interpreting Scripture in harmony with the rest of Scripture

modules.title: Reading Different Kinds of Writing
modules.intro: The Bible contains narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, parables and letters. Each is read a little differently.

lessons.title: Narrative and law
lessons.body:
**Narrative** tells what happened. Not everything recorded is approved: David's sin with Bathsheba is told as a warning (2 Samuel 11-12). Look for the lesson the story teaches about God and people, and check it against direct teaching elsewhere (1 Corinthians 10:11).

**Law** shows God's holiness and the shape of a godly life. Some laws were for Israel's worship and national life and are fulfilled in Christ, such as sacrifices and food laws (Hebrews 10:1; Mark 7:19). The moral principles, summed up in love for God and neighbour, still guide us (Matthew 22:37-40).

lessons.title: Poetry, wisdom and prophecy
lessons.body:
**Poetry** (Psalms, Song of Solomon) uses images and parallel lines. "The LORD is my shepherd" is a picture of care, not a statement that we are sheep.

**Wisdom** (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Job) gives general principles. Proverbs 22:6 describes what usually happens when a child is trained well; it is wisdom, not a guaranteed promise in every case.

**Prophecy** includes calls to repent, promises and predictions. Some were fulfilled in Israel's history, some in Christ's first coming, some await His return. Interpret prophecy by its fulfilment in the New Testament where possible (Acts 2:16-21).

lessons.title: Parables and letters
lessons.body:
**Parables** are short stories with a main point, often a surprise. Jesus explained some details (Matthew 13:18-23), but we should not press every detail into a hidden meaning. Ask: what is the main lesson, and to whom was it told (Luke 15:1-3)?

**Letters** (epistles) are written to real churches about real problems. Read them as whole arguments; follow the reasoning. Ask what the original readers were told to believe and do, then what principle carries over to us.

When the reason given is timeless (such as God's character or creation), the command carries over directly.

terms.def: A kind of writing, such as narrative, poetry, prophecy or letter.
Writing that tells a story of events.
The Hebrew poetic habit of repeating or contrasting an idea in two lines.
A short story told by Jesus to teach a main spiritual point.
Treating every detail of a text as a hidden symbol, beyond what the author meant.
The coming to pass of what was promised or predicted.

texts.teaches: Old Testament events were written as examples for our warning.
All the law hangs on love for God and neighbour.
Training a child in the right way usually shapes the whole life.
Peter explained Pentecost as fulfilling Joel's prophecy.
Jesus explained the parable of the sower to His disciples.

summary: Narrative describes; not everything recorded is approved.
Laws for Israel's worship are fulfilled in Christ; moral principles remain.
Poetry uses images; proverbs give general wisdom, not guarantees.
Find the main point of parables; follow the argument of letters.

questions.q: Why is David's sin with Bathsheba recorded?
options: As a warning, not an example to follow

questions.q: Proverbs are best read as:
options: General wisdom about how life usually works

questions.q: What is allegorising?
options: Making every detail a hidden symbol beyond the author's meaning
Finding the main point of a parable

questions.q: How should we interpret prophecy where possible?
options: By its fulfilment shown in the New Testament

modules.title: Application: How Should I Live?
modules.intro: Interpretation is not complete until the truth is lived. This week we learn to apply Scripture faithfully, and to avoid common errors.

lessons.title: From then to now
lessons.body:
Application builds a bridge from the original setting to ours. Three steps help:

1. **What did it mean to them?** State the meaning for the first readers.
2. **What is the timeless principle?** Find the truth about God and people behind it.
3. **How does it apply to me now?** Bring that principle into today's choices.

For example, Paul's instruction about meat offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8) teaches the principle of not using our freedom in a way that makes a weaker believer stumble. That applies to many modern situations.

lessons.title: Common errors to avoid
lessons.body:
- **Proof-texting:** quoting a verse out of context to support an idea.
- **Allegorising:** inventing hidden meanings for every detail.
- **Spiritualising promises** made to a specific person or nation without asking how they apply.
- **Reading experience into the text:** "It must mean this, because it happened to me."
- **Ignoring the whole Bible:** building a doctrine on one verse.

Jesus corrected the Sadducees: "Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God" (Matthew 22:29).

lessons.title: Study that changes us
lessons.body:
The goal of Bible study is not information but transformation. "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth" (John 17:17). We are changed into Christ's image as we behold His glory in the Word (2 Corinthians 3:18).

End each study by asking: Is there a sin to confess, a promise to trust, a command to obey, an example to follow, or a truth about God to worship?

Then share it. Teaching others is one of the best ways to learn (2 Timothy 2:2).

terms.def: Bringing a passage's meaning into present belief and practice.
The lasting truth behind a command or event, which carries over to today.
Using a verse out of context to support an idea.
Being changed into Christ's likeness through the truth.
The first people to whom a book or letter was written.
Treating a literal or specific statement as a general spiritual promise without warrant.

texts.teaches: Do not let your liberty become a stumbling block to the weak.
What was written before was written for our learning and hope.
Error comes from not knowing the Scriptures or God's power.
Beholding the Lord's glory, believers are changed into His image.
Commit what you have learned to faithful people who can teach others.

summary: Apply in three steps: meaning then, timeless principle, application now.
Avoid proof-texting, allegorising and building doctrine on one verse.
Aim for transformation, not just information.
Ask what to confess, trust, obey, follow or worship, and share it.

questions.q: What is the second step in applying a passage?
What is proof-texting?
options: Quoting a verse out of context to support an idea

questions.q: What principle comes from 1 Corinthians 8?
options: Do not use your freedom to make a weaker believer stumble

questions.q: According to Matthew 22:29, why did the Sadducees err?
options: They did not know the Scriptures nor God's power

short.q: What is the difference between exegesis and eisegesis?
short.model: Exegesis draws the meaning out of the text; eisegesis reads one's own ideas into it.

short.q: Why is context so important in interpretation?
short.model: Because the surrounding words, passage and book determine a verse's meaning; without context a verse can be twisted to mean almost anything.

short.q: How do Romans 3:28 and James 2:24 fit together?
short.model: We are justified before God by faith alone, and true faith is shown to be real by works; saving faith is a working faith.
As general wisdom about how life usually works, not as guaranteed promises for every case.

short.q: What three steps help apply a passage today?
short.model: Ask what it meant to the original readers, find the timeless principle, and apply that principle to life now.

short.q: Why should a doctrine not be built on a single verse?
short.model: Because Scripture must be read as a whole; gathering all it says keeps doctrine balanced and in harmony with the rest of the Bible.

lists.q: List the three steps of the Bible study method taught in this course.
List four kinds of writing (genres) found in the Bible.
List three common errors in interpretation.

assignments.title: Study a passage
assignments.prompt: Choose one of these passages: Psalm 23, Luke 15:11-32, or Philippians 2:1-11. Write up your study in three sections: Observation (what it says), Interpretation (what it means in context, with at least two cross-references), and Application (how it applies today).

assignments.title: Correcting a misused verse
assignments.prompt: Choose a verse you have heard used out of context (for example Jeremiah 29:11, Matthew 18:20 or Philippians 4:13). Explain how it is commonly used, what it means in its context, and how it can be applied faithfully.

reading: Gordon D. Fee and Douglas Stuart, How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth
